title: Don't give the groom a drink
translation: Be careful about giving drink to servants.

A man who lived in Uji was on close terms with his brother-in-law Gukakubō, a refined priest in the capital who had left the world. One day he sent a horse to fetch him. "It's a long way," said Gukakubō. "Give the groom a drink first." Sake was brought, and the groom held out his cup again and again and gulped it down.

He had a sword at his hip and looked like he could handle himself, so Gukakubō felt safe and set off with him. Near Kohata, on the road south, they met a party of priests from Nara with a lot of armed men. The groom stepped out in front of them. "Mountains, after dark? That's suspicious. Halt!" And he drew his sword. They all drew their swords too and put arrows to their bows. Gukakubō rubbed his hands together and begged: "He's drunk out of his mind. Please, I beg you, let it go." They sneered at the two of them and went past.

Then the groom turned on Gukakubō. "Your Reverence, that was a rotten thing to do. I'm not drunk. I was about to make my name, and you made me put my sword away for nothing." In a rage, he slashed him down off the horse.

Then he started shouting, "Bandits! Bandits!" The villagers came running out, and he yelled, "I'm the bandit!" and ran at them, slashing in every direction, until there were enough of them to wound him, knock him down and tie him up.

The horse, covered in blood, galloped back to the house on the main street in Uji. The master was horrified and sent a lot of men running. They found Gukakubō lying in a patch of gardenia bushes, groaning, and carried him home. He lived, just about. But the sword had caught him at the hip, and he was crippled for life.

literal: Making servants drink sake is something to be careful about.
A man who lived in Uji, since a refined priest who had left the world, called Gukakubō, in the capital, was his brother-in-law, was always on intimate terms with him.

One time, when he sent a horse to fetch him, (Gukakubō) said, 'It is a long way; first have the groom (drink) once', and when sake was brought out, (the groom) held out (his cup) again and again and drank it down gulping.
Since he wore a sword at his side and looked capable, (Gukakubō) felt reassured and took him along; while they were going, around Kohata, they met Nara priests with many soldiers, and

this man stood facing them and said, 'In the mountains when the day has grown dark, (you are) suspicious. Halt!', and drew his sword; when the others too all drew swords and fitted arrows and the like, Gukakubō rubbed his hands together and said, 'He is a person drunk out of his senses. Please, I beg you, forgive him', and they each sneered and went past.
This man turned to Gukakubō: 'Your Reverence has done a regrettable thing.
I am not at all drunk.
I was about to perform a deed of valour, and you made my drawn sword useless', he said in anger, and slashed him down with all his might.

Then, when he shouted, 'There are bandits!', the villagers rose up and came out together, and he said, 'I am the bandit!' and ran at them and went about slashing; many of them together wounded him, knocked him down and tied him up.
The horse, covered in blood, ran into the house on the main street of Uji.
Shocked, (the master) sent many men running, and they searched out Gukakubō, who was lying groaning in a field of gardenias, and carried him back.
He barely kept his life, but he was cut at the hips and injured, and became crippled.

notes.text: {下部|しもべ}: servants, lower staff. のまする: the attributive form of のます, 'to make (someone) drink'. The section opens with the moral and then tells the story that proves it.
{小舅|こじうと}: a brother-in-law, usually the wife's brother. So the man in Uji had probably married Gukakubō's sister.
{遁世|とんせい}: 'escaping the world'. Gukakubō was a priest who had left ordinary life, as Kenkō himself had. なまめく: 'refined, elegant'.
The groom who walks at the horse's head and leads it by the rope at its mouth (口). Gukakubō rides, the groom walks.

notes.quote: さしうけさしうけよよと飲みぬ
notes.text: さしうく: to hold out one's cup for more. Doubled, it means again and again. よよ: the sound of gulping. まづ{一度|ひとたび}せさせよ, 'have him do it once first', was meant as one polite drink.

Kohata, on the road south from Kyoto towards Uji and Nara, with wooded hills on both sides. {奈良|なら}{法師|ほふし}: priests from the big Nara temples such as Kōfukuji and Tōdaiji, which kept armed men of their own.
Rubbing the palms together: the gesture of someone begging for mercy. {現心|うつしごころ}なく: 'without his right mind'.

A false friend: {高名|かうみやう} here is a deed of valour, glory won in a fight. Modern {高名|こうめい} just means 'famous'. つかまつる: humble 'to do'. The drunk groom still speaks politely to the priest while he blames him.
He shouts 'Bandits!' himself, and then, when the villagers come, announces that he is the bandit. こそ here has no 結び: the sentence just ends in よ.

notes.quote: 梔原にによび伏したる
notes.text: {梔|くちなし}: gardenia. によぶ: 'to groan'. からき{命|いのち}: 'a bitter life', that is, he only just survived. かたは: crippled, disabled.
